newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical sector pay talks postponed.
newsitem.headline: German chemical sector pay talks postponed.

text.p: German wage negotiations in the chemical sector were adjourned on Tuesday after six fruitless hours and will continue on December 5 in Hanover, a spokesman for the IG Chemie union said.
Both sides blamed each other for the break-down in talks, which are part of the overall 1997 wage round for 590,000 west German chemical sector employees.
Wider wage talks have been brought forward to allow scope for talks on sick pay, which threatens to disrupt normally-good relations in the industry.

"We disagreed very strongly," Hans Terbrack, chief negotiator for IG Chemie, said. There were major differences between the two sides and Terbrack questioned whether or not a solution was even possible.
Terbrack reiterated the IG Chemie position that it is only ready to reach agreement in the dispute if full sick pay continues to be paid.
IG Chemie said that employers maintained that the number of sick days was too high, which had led to the cutting of sick pay, which IG Chemie said was a shocking assertion.

Ludwig Georg Braun, spokesman for the employers, said that if no agreement was reached soon, more companies would cut sick pay, to which Terbrack replied: "If that happens, then the companies will again have disruption in the factories."

The IG Chemie trade union had earlier said it would be going into the talks seeking a 4.2 percent overall rise in wages, reflecting productivity growth of 2.7 percent in the industry and an estimated 1.5 percent rate of inflation.
But leaders of the BAVC chemical employers federation said they did not accept the level of the productivity rise because it had only been obtained as a result of job cuts.

Both IG Chemie and DAG, the white-collar workers union, stressed that they would be seeking to retain full sick pay entitlements, which under a new law would be cut to 80 percent of salary from 100 percent.
Wage contracts for the chemical workers do not specifically protect sick pay at 100 percent of salary in the same way that metal and engineering unions argue that contracts in their sectors do.

Nonetheless, a recent attempt by BASF AG to implement the cuts led to mass protests from its workers in an industry that normally prides itself on being able swiftly to come to agreements between employers and workers.
IG Chemie said it was willing to consider reductions in holiday bonuses in an overall agreement as long as full sick pay entitlements were secured.
The BAVC said last month that companies would have to decide for themselves whether they would implement the sick pay cuts until a sector-wide agreement could be found.
IG Chemie said late last month that it knew of no large company that had so far sought to put the new law into effect.
The talks are due to continue on Tuesday.
